messages.author: 73f23d5a39905842
messages.subject: Deer Spotlight Data & Distance Sampling
parts:
Dear Distance Users,

I recently started a new position which includes monitoring the refuge
white-tail deer herd (at least the portion of the Missouri herd that occurs
on and adjacent to the refuge). In the past, starting in 1988, refuge
staff have conducted spotlight surveys on 2 preselected routes (21.3 km
and 12.4 km) on the refuge. In my opinion these routes cover all of the
representative habitats and allow spotlighters to cover somewhere around
40% of the refuge proper (18,379 ha). Early on they just counted deer per
km and last year they began to take distance estimates - guessing distance
in meters. This year we are running the routes again and using laser range
finders to obtain accurate distances. I would like to be able to analyze
this data using program DISTANCE, if possible, with the goal of obtaining
density estimates with reasonable CVs and confidence limits that can be
used over the long term for trend estimates. My questions are as follows:
1) The deer occur in all sizes of groups from 1 - 8+ and sometimes in what
could be termed as loose aggregations, depending on the time of year, so
should I model for clusters or individuals? 2) Is it statistically sound
to use multiple samples of the same routes, over time, to increase transect
sample size? It appears that this is necessary as spotlight effectiveness
changes depending on time of year - such as buck prevalence during the rut
versus late winter. We plan to run each route twice before general
firearms hunting, twice after, and twice late winter (post muzzle loader
season) for a total of 12 transects. 3) Has anyone tried this with deer
spotlighting and if so do you have any advice on design and analysis? The
sample size for our first survey this year for total number of groups
spotted has been n= 174 and the total number of deer has been n= 315.
These are comparable to previous years data. 4) Do these sample sizes
appear large enough to make distance sampling techniques useful? I greatly
appreciate any help or references that anyone can provide. Thank you in
advance for your time.
=================================
Frank Durbian
Wildlife Biologist
Squaw Creek National Wildlife Refuge
PO Box 158
Mound City, MO 64470-0158
660-442-5754 Ext. 17
=================================

messages.author: 3908a2da5354fc44
messages.subject: Re: Deer Spotlight Data & Distance Sampling
parts:
Frank,

>From my experience, the problem with conducting spotlight surveys for deer is
that you are restricted to conducting surveys from the road, and deer usually
are not randomly located with respect to roads. First, you wouldn't
necessarily expect a deer to be close to the road (even if they are in an
adjoining field). Second, usually roads adjoin fields or food sources that
attract deer relative to the overall landscape.

Other people can probably answer your other questions better, but here's my
$0.02.

1. If possible, try to come up with an a priori definition of a group. My
understanding that analyzing the data as individuals won't necessarily
introduce a lot of bias in your estimates, but if possible, analyze the data by
groups.

2. Repeated surveys should be appropriate if analyzed as replicates. However,
I have noticed that multiple nights of spotlighting cause changes in deer
behavior (i.e., each night fewer deer are observed close to the road).

3. See my comments above

4. It appears you can collect enough data to develop a sightability curve, but
the real issue is whether your transect placement appropriately samples the
population.

Good luck,

Duane Diefenbach
USGS/BRD
PA Coop. Fish and Wildlife Research Unit
Penn State University

messages.author: f7f37ba01b5461a2
messages.subject: Re: Deer Spotlight Data & Distance Sampling
parts:
Mr. Durbian,

There are several points to consider pertaining to sample design and deer
autecology.

1. The perpendicular distances must be accurate. Guessing the distance and
where the perpendicular intersects the transect line is very inaccurate, but
can presumably be overcome with large sample sizes (see Knick and Dyer 1997).
The method described by Gill et al. 1997 will yield inaccurate distances from
non-linear transects (roads; draw an "s" shaped transect and demonstrate this
to yourself). I recommend the method of Pierce 2000, which uses GIS to extract
perpendicular distances from non-linear transects using range, bearing, and
observer location (UTM coordinates) data.

2. Getting a good distance function fit is important. Large data sets are
ideal, but not always available. If you are setting up a monitoring program
from scratch, then as data begins to accumulate over time you may be able to
combine the distance data for the purposes of obtaining a good detection
function fit.. Presumably you are acquiring data from the same area under the
same conditions on a yearly basis, and therefore the detection variables are
assumed to be the same from year to year. Density is then estimated separately
for each year.

3. In my experience, white-tailed deer generally avoid the area immediately
adjacent to roadways. Our data from both scrub oak savannahs and hardwood
forest indicate that deer avoid roadways, presumably to avoid the disturbance
generated by traffic. This is apparent when histograms of the raw distance
data are evaluated. As suggested by Buckland et al. (1993) the only way to
pragmatically cope with this problem is by curve smoothing (using the distance
data as frequency class intervals). As such your data would be analyzed as
groups using a frequency interval dictated by inspection of the distance data
histograms. Again, a large number of observations will make this step very
easy to accomplish.

4. You can use repeated counts along the same line, as long as the counts are
independent (ie. counting each group only once per sample effort). This is not
the ideal sample design but it is unavoidable in some circumstances. This was
discussed in recent postings to the list, and is discussed at length in Pierce
2000 and Gill et al. 1997.

5. Roads should not be used as transects whenever this is possible. However,
if roads are used then they must adequately represent cover/habitat types
within the study area. This can be determined using GIS to examine the
proportion of each cover/habitat type along the transects versus the
proportion of the same cover/habitat types within the study area.

6. The time of year when the counts are conducted is of great importance.
While most state and federal agencies conduct white-tailed deer surveys during
the fall to maximize counts when foliar density is low (McCullough 1982),
sexual differences in habitat utilization are at a minimum during the late
summer to early fall time frame (Downing et al. 1977, McCullough 1982, Beier
and McCullough 1990, and McCullough et al. 1994). In addition, white-tailed
deer activities patterns approach their diel maximum 1/2 to 1 hour before dark
(Downing et al. 1977, McCullough 1982, Beier and McCullough 1990, and
McCullough et al. 1994). So if you are trying to determine density and herd
composition simultaneously, then the late summer-early fall time frame is
recommended. If you are only concerned with density, then fall surveys may
yield the most observations per unit effort.

Brian L. Pierce
Wildlife Biologist
SWTSU
imh...@mo-net.com

====================

composition simultaneously, then the late summer-early fall time frame is
recommended. If you are only concerned with density, then fall surveys may
yield the most observations per unit effort.

Brian L. Pierce
Wildlife Biologist

messages.subject: Re: Deer Spotlight Data & Distance Sampling
parts:
Mr. Durbian,

There are several points to consider pertaining to sample design and deer
autecology.

1. The perpendicular distances must be accurate. Guessing the distance and
where the perpendicular intersects the transect line is very inaccurate, but
can presumably be overcome with large sample sizes (see Knick and Dyer 1997).
The method described by Gill et al. 1997 will yield inaccurate distances from
non-linear transects (roads; draw an "s" shaped transect and demonstrate this
to yourself). I recommend the method of Pierce 2000, which uses GIS to extract
perpendicular distances from non-linear transects using range, bearing, and
observer location (UTM coordinates) data.

2. Getting a good distance function fit is important. Large data sets are
ideal, but not always available. If you are setting up a monitoring program
from scratch, then as data begins to accumulate over time you may be able to
combine the distance data for the purposes of obtaining a good detection
function fit.. Presumably you are acquiring data from the same area under the
same conditions on a yearly basis, and therefore the detection variables are
assumed to be the same from year to year. Density is then estimated separately
for each year.

3. In my experience, white-tailed deer generally avoid the area immediately
adjacent to roadways. Our data from both scrub oak savannahs and hardwood
forest indicate that deer avoid roadways, presumably to avoid the disturbance
generated by traffic. This is apparent when histograms of the raw distance
data are evaluated. As suggested by Buckland et al. (1993) the only way to
pragmatically cope with this problem is by curve smoothing (using the distance
data as frequency class intervals). As such your data would be analyzed as
groups using a frequency interval dictated by inspection of the distance data
histograms. Again, a large number of observations will make this step very
easy to accomplish.

4. You can use repeated counts along the same line, as long as the counts are
independent (ie. counting each group only once per sample effort). This is not
the ideal sample design but it is unavoidable in some circumstances. This was
discussed in recent postings to the list, and is discussed at length in Pierce
2000 and Gill et al. 1997.

5. Roads should not be used as transects whenever this is possible. However,
if roads are used then they must adequately represent cover/habitat types
within the study area. This can be determined using GIS to examine the
proportion of each cover/habitat type along the transects versus the
proportion of the same cover/habitat types within the study area.

6. The time of year when the counts are conducted is of great importance.
While most state and federal agencies conduct white-tailed deer surveys during
the fall to maximize counts when foliar density is low (McCullough 1982),
sexual differences in habitat utilization are at a minimum during the late
summer to early fall time frame (Downing et al. 1977, McCullough 1982, Beier
and McCullough 1990, and McCullough et al. 1994). In addition, white-tailed
deer activities patterns approach their diel maximum 1/2 to 1 hour before dark
(Downing et al. 1977, McCullough 1982, Beier and McCullough 1990, and
McCullough et al. 1994). So if you are trying to determine density and herd
composition simultaneously, then the late summer-early fall time frame is
recommended. If you are only concerned with density, then fall surveys may
yield the most observations per unit effort.

Brian L. Pierce
Wildlife Biologist
SWTSU
